description: Baby squirrel on front lawn, ( pine trees line our street) dehydrated, bit of blood coming from one nostril, very weak.  Neighbor had seen it on his wall day before.  No mother in sight and didn't come to retrieve squirrel when placed on lawn in the sun. Took baby in, gave it Pedialyte for 24 hrs. Then started on Esbilac formula.  Another baby squirrel seen on pine tree, left it alone. Watched it make it up tree, then it fell to the lawn.  It ran up to me!  Tried to get into house, climbed up screen, then went into house under screen.  Showed 2nd squirrel the 1st squirrel and he jumped onto hand and nestled with 1st squirrel.  Gave 2nd squirrel Pedialyte 24 hrs. then Esbilac.  Husband built large cage, put it in sun in front yard with the 2 male babies.  A third baby squirrel, a female, crying in front yard, running around near cage.  I picked it up it put in cage with first two.  Raised them to release age and weight.  They now roam our trees and come to us for walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, and a crushed rodent block mixture I make with powdered milk for toddlers, applesauce and crushed nuts.  They also eat oranges, grapes, blackberries, pomegranate seeds.  An old man at other end of street saw me feeding them and informed me he traps squirrel and takes them on a "one way ride" up to the mountains.  He said he would take "mine" if caught!  He said we are "being overrun by squirrels."  Not!  He keeps trap on parkway by the sidewalk (city property) near his house.  I have released squirrels from his trap three times.  I don't know if they are "mine" or not, and I don't know if it was the same squirrel the three times or not.  I read they have 80% to 100% chance of dying when relocated.  There have been squirrels in our neighborhood and surrounding neighborhoods for years.  I haven't seen more than 3 or four occupying my street. ( Every year these neighborhood squirrels get into our very large avocado tree and take bites out of the avocados.)  I suspect he had trapped "my" squirrels' mother and that's why they were running around alone and unafraid of people.  I did see one large male chasing "my" squirrels into the avocado tree.  I have not seen this one for about a month.   Sadly, at this writing I have not seen "my" female for a day and a half, and at 8:25 a.m I have yet to see the two males either.  The trap down the street is empty, though.   These three nest together right now since they are only about 5 months old.  The only vocalizations they make are squeaks when one chases another away when I am offering them food.  Sometimes they are all three together, most times one male with the female, more often the two males together.  The female has, on a couple of occasions, not showed up for a day.  They have occupied an abandoned barn owl nest high up in a pine tree in front of our house.  They go there at sundown for the night.  They also have a drey in a tall tree in our back yard. The squirrels and birds like to hang around the pool and gym area because it offers some cover from predators and threats. The solitary squirrel seemed to have adapted to the urban environment as it showed no hesitation in approaching me directly because I was eating Cheerios. Squirrels are very interesting and never stop to fascinate me. They maybe common but I like them but not when they deliberately destroy my peanut and seed feeders. They cause a lot of trouble for a lot of birders and bird watchers that keep backyard feeding stations. If you do have a feeder station you might want to conceder making or buying a few squirrel only feeders if you want to prevent a ruckus. A fun fact about squirrels is that you might see them normally as very happy with seeds and nuts however they have been known to eat meat and raid bird nests for eggs. They will also eat fruit from time to time. They are interesting when it comes to eating habits. Squirrels are pirates too and will often steal another ones booty seeds is the normal case. Squirrels will burry and nut and sometimes under intense study from another squirrel. However some squirrels will actually outsmart other squirrels by dummy hiding a nut and move off to hide the nut in another location leaving an empty pit for another squirrel. Squirrels can be fiercely territorial and often fight with others.

description:
White Rock lake, Winsted parking lot 
Mockingbird vs Squirrel 
 Sharing an amazing experience I had that took place in 5 seconds of time. 
Photo 1: 
I was about to get in my car and leave the lake when I heard a commotion coming in my direction. I barely had time to grab my camera and get a few shots as these two came by me at a very high speed. Lots of blur but I'm just happy to have successfully captured what I did. I don't know what the squirrel did to piss off the mockingbird but the mocker was making all kinds of racket as it had the squirrel running like its life depended on escaping. Interesting how the shadow of the bird shows more detail than the bird itself. 
Photo 2: 
Past the parking lot and into the grass, I thought the squirrel would go up the tree but it did not. The mockingbird was still pursuing and squawking loudly. The action was so fast I'm still amazed I got any photos. 
Photo 3: 
The squirrel doubled back and the mockingbird overshot and ended up on the other side of the tree. However, this did not end the chase. 
Photo 4: 
Instead of running up the tree, the squirrel took off again away from the tree and the mockingbird started to get close again. 
Photo 5: 
Abruptly the squirrel changes direction and the mockingbird overshoots again. I still can't believe what I am seeing. There must be a fledgling mockingbird on the ground for the parent to be so relentless. Right after this shot, the squirrel made a mad dash around the corner of the building. The bird corrected its course, then decided to stop the pursuit with the squirrel out of sight. The mockingbird flew up into the tree. I peeked around the corner of the building but there was no sign of the squirrel. Wisely, it had left the premises. Later I checked the time stamps & was surprised to find this action took place in exactly 5 seconds of time.

description:
Behavior series, one of the funniest things I've ever seen.
Disastrous Mating Attempt 
Photo 1:  I looked out my window and saw a squirrel drinking from the only water not frozen.  Suddenly another squirrel rushed across the yard, up the fountain, grabbed her as she was drinking & attempted to mate with her.
Photo 2:  The problem was, it was slippery and his weight was dragging them both towards the cold water.
Photo 3:  Already their tails were getting wet with little icicles forming in the fur.
Photo 4:  At this point she was starting to look a bit alarmed and he was desperately trying to hold on.  His hind foot was slipping off the faux rock.
Photo 5:  Now her front feet started slipping and she was fighting to hold on.
Photo 6:  He has lost traction and is started to fall and is dragging her down with him because he is unwilling to let go.  Notice how tightly he has her around her middle.  
Photo 7:  At this moment, both squirrels lost their grip and begin to fall into the frigid water.  Look close and you can see where she made one last desperate grab with 2 toes but could not find traction on the frozen surface.
Photo 8:  This was the last shot I got just before they both hit the water and exploded out of the fountain with water being slung everywhere as they broke apart and scrambled up a tree.  I was laughing so hard I missed the shutter and did not get that shot. This entire sequence of 8 shots took place over 11 seconds.

description:
This squirrel is hilarious. I watch our fruit trees but I do not get aggressive. This one knows I am here but really wants fruit (and usually gets it). This morning, it was vocalizing continuously from a spot in the neighboring yard while looking into ours, and specifically toward the fig tree. I finally went outside to see about the commotion. This squirrel rarely vocalizes in my experience, so I wondered if there was a cat or a raptor around. But I could find no third-party agitating the squirrel. It seemed focused solely on me and the fig tree. It was clearly challenged yet determined to come into my yard and I venture that that’s what got it yammering. It stared at the fig and made persistent noise. When I came closer to the fig, the squirrel ran into several fence-line trees and seem to be having a little tantrum, biting at branches and moving erratically. Then it dropped to the backside of the fence (maybe hoping I would go away - instead, I took a photo). It remained there, very still as though trying to be invisible. I went back into the house and the vocalizing resumed, with the squirrel jumping into a fig-adjacent tree and finally making the big leap over. It got its fruit and retreated back to the fence. Less than ten minutes later, I heard it vocalizing in the front yard where there is another fig and pomegranate. Sorry, I didn’t investigate. Enough squirrel telenovela for this morning.
Btw, once it has its fruit, it doesn’t seem bothered by me at all. Prior to getting the fruit, if I approach, it will often freeze as though its motionlessness makes me unable to see it.

description: Fox squirrels are a diurnal, non-territorial, solitary species that reside in forest patches and urban neighborhoods within the Eastern United States. They shelter in self-made leaf nests or dreys and tree dens. Their diet consists of acorns, (mast), insects, tubers, fruits,etc. They bury food items for later consumption and energy conservation. Cohabitation is frequent, but overall they are solitary creatures and only come together during breeding season. Fox squirrels have a large vocabulary of sounds that they use to communicate with. They are impressive jumpers and agile climbers. When threatened, they stiffen their tail and flick it in the air. This species can have 2 litters of offspring a year, and sexually mature around 11 months old. The average clutch or litter size is 3 individuals. Parental care is high in this species and they take care of their young for about 13 weeks until the offspring disperse on their own.

description:
Amazing encounter between a hawk and a squirrel at my home. Please scroll thru the shots to see the squirrel this observation is for.  Needed to keep the story in order. Did one for the hawk already.

Photo 1: 
All of the action in this 16 part story took place in 4 minutes in very low light at the furthest away from my window part of my front yard. I happened to glance out and saw the mature cooper's hawk on my fence and thought I'd take a few shots. Here it is calmly perched with one foot tucked up for warmth. The time was 4:49pm on a cloudy day. 
Photo 2: 
When the hawk looked down I checked and there was a squirrel feeding on the ground. The birds were all in hiding. I was not worried, the cooper's usually take white-winged doves for their prey at my home and the squirrels simply leave when they notice a hawk. Time stamp still says 4:49pm. 
Photo 3: 
I was focused on the hawk and when it turned its gaze in this direction, I just figured it was looking for prey. I later realized that the squirrel had spotted the hawk and was making its way to the fence towards it. This time stamp says 4:51pm. 
Photo 4: 
It was at this point that I realized what was going on and pulled my camera back to include more of the area so the squirrel could be seen. It had climbed the fence and seemed to be advancing on the hawk. I thought for sure the squirrel was a goner and lacking in intelligence. Time stamp still says 4:51. 
Photo 5: 
I was holding my breath as the squirrel continued to go towards the hawk. Time stamp still says 4:51. 
Photo 6: 
The squirrel has the full attention of the hawk and continues to advance. Mind you, this is a mature hawk, not an inexperienced juvenile. Time stamp still says 4:51. 
Photo 7: 
This part happened so fast I only caught a glimpse of the action. The hawk is completely in the air and off the fence like it was trying to pounce on the squirrel. You can just see the end of the squirrels tail as it leaped on the roof. Time stamp says 4:52. 
Photo 8: 
The hawk landed on the fence, all flustered still and facing the backyard. I figured the squirrel was long gone. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 9: 
The hawk calms down and its feathers smooth and I figured the action was all over. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 10: 
I had zoomed back in on the hawk when its head suddenly snapped to the left. Turns out the darn squirrel was climbing up the fence again from the back side at the gap between gate and fence. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 11: 
I zoomed back out again and got this shot of the hawk going ballistic and you can barely see the squirrel in the gap as it dives down again. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 12: 
Here the hawk is looking down at the squirrel which is apparently starting to climb up the fence again. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 13: 
As the squirrel which I could not see yet, get higher, the hawk gets more agitated and raises its wings higher to look more threatening I assume. The gaze of the hawk is directed slightly higher too. Time stamp still says 4:52. 
Photo 14: 
As you can see from the hawks gaze, the squirrel has almost reached the top of the fence, not in the gap this time but on the section closer to the brick. The hawks wings are higher still and the tail feathers are stretched out. Hawk making itself look even bigger. Time stamp still says 4:52, this was all happening in a very short amount of time. I was clicking away. 
Photo 15: 
If you look at the top of the fence where it touches the brick you can see where the squirrel has put one paw on the top. The hawk reacted by spreading its wings and tail as far as they can go. It was more than the hawk could take. What happened next was that the hawk took off so quick I did not get it and flew to the back so was out of sight immediately. Time stamp here is still 4:52. 
Photo 16: 
I took my eye away from the camera and looked at the sky to see if the hawk was on the roof or a tree or circling in the air but the hawk had left the area. I looked back at the fence and there was the squirrel trotting down to where the hawk had been sitting. It jumped down in the front yard and ran up my pecan tree. It had successfully run the hawk off. Apparently I have some ballsy squirrels. The time stamp here is 4:53. On all my photos in my gallery you can look below right of a photo and see a small letter I in a circle and click on it and you get the camera exif which includes timestamps if you don't believe me. :) I'll probably never see something like this again, it was pretty awesome.

description:
Normal vs ocd method of eating a green pecan
Photo 1:
Eating a Green Pecan
Squirrels will eat unripe, green pecans.  This squirrel demonstrates the quick and easy way to eat a green pecan.  You bite one end off and then chow down on the insides full of unripe, white, squishy pecan.
Photo 2:
OCD Squirrel Eating A Green Pecan
A little while later I saw this squirrel demonstrating another way to eat a green pecan.  The OCD way.  First you take the green pecan and you turn it around and around as you carefully peel off the green hull.  
Photo 3:
Methodically Removing Unripe Shell
Once the green outer hull is gone, you continue spinning the pecan as you work on removing the soft shell.  
Photo 4:
Every Little Bit Must Go
Even though the meat of the pecan is showing at one end, the ocd squirrel does not stop until she gnaws every last bit of the soft shell off the nut.
Photo 5:
Finally Taking A Bite
Once all the shell was carefully peeled off, the squirrel took the first bite.  
Photo 6:
Enjoying The Fruits Of My Labor
She seemed to really be enjoying that unripe pecan.  For someone so particular regarding peeling it, she sure is a messy eater.

description:
11 part photo story
Separation Anxiety
Photo 1:
A mother squirrel brought her baby to the feeding area of my yard for the first time.  The baby had some anxiety issues and seemed to need to stay touching mommy at all times.  This was when I first saw them with baby trying to hide under mommy's tail.
Photo 2:
Mom is tired and wants to rest but the kid is all over her, desperate to stay touching her for security.
Photo 3:
No matter what direction the mom turns, the kid has to keep a paw on her.  
Photo 4:
Looks like mom is asking for help.  I'm sure all mothers know exactly how she feels.  I remember that clingy toddler stage.
Photo 5:
I must have made a sudden movement because all of a sudden they were both looking at me.  For once the baby was too startled to hang onto mom.  
Photo 6:
Mom is about to jump up and climb a tree.  Baby is panicking and seems to be saying don't leave me. 
Photo 7:
Even up in the tree, baby stayed under mom's tail with its nose right up her, well, you know.  Right about now mom spotted something on the ground and jumped down, leaving baby traumatized in the tree. 
Photo 8:
Mom jumped down from the tree because a second baby squirrel had showed up and was making a loud crying sound.  The minute she was back on the sidewalk, baby two was all over her with a panicked look in its eyes.  No wonder mom is so tired.  Meanwhile, baby #1 is starting to panic up in the tree.  
Photo 9:
While mom was on the ground with baby #2 plastered to her, baby #1 was stuck in the tree not sure how to get down and watching mom and sibling below.
Photo 10:
While baby #1 was stuck up in the tree, baby #2 felt it necessary to get all 4 paws touching mom.
Photo 11:
This was the last shot I got of this before I got called away.  This is still baby #2  with mom.  Somehow baby 1 got down from the tree or mom and sibling joined it, they were gone when I returned.  So funny how the baby squirrels act when they are brought to the food area the first time.

Blue Eyes Have Turned Red As The Blond Squirrel Grows Up
The unusual blond baby squirrel is growing up and those pretty blue eyes are changing to something still different. NUMBER: 20191231
SPECIES: Fox Squirrel, Sciurus niger Linnaeus,1758[1]
SUBSPECIES: Big Cypress Fox Squirrel, Sciurus niger avicennia Howell, 1919
SIZE, CONDITION, SEX: adult, melanistic, possibly female (see belly in Fig. A; verses #36160838, Fig. C).
DISTINCTIONS FROM 1ST MELANISTIC ANIMAL: Appeared to be more melanistic; Ears, face, and front paws with much less white; tail margins white unlike uniform color in 1st; apparently slightly smaller. 
DATE, TIME, DURATION: 31 December 2019, 10:00 am, 20 min
LOCALITIES: (A) NE corner of Fishtail Lake to (B) putting course, Lely Palms
LATITUDE, LONGITUDE: (A) 26°6’23.8” N, -81°42’52.2” W (26.1066, -81.7145) to (B) 26°6’27.4” N, -81°42’45.4” W (26.1076, -81.7126)

COMMENTS: This animal appears to be different from the first melanistic animal we reported (Williams and Bunkley-Williams, 2019).  Possibly the first, larger, melanistic individual was a male and the second a female.

description:
This is a tree squirrel I came across on my walk. It must be used to seeing humans because it did not run away as I got near. Tree squirrels are the most 
 common, bushy-tailed squirrels in North America, Europe, temperate Asia, Central America and South America. This squirrel in particular does not need to fear predators because it resides in more or a residential area. This squirrel was also accompanied by a squirrel friend (not pictured). Tree squirrels live till 12 years and based on the appearance of this squirrel it looks like it is in the mating phase of its life so it is appropriate to assume that the squirrel friend it was with was its mating partner. As you can probably infer based off its name, this squirrels habit is in trees. Due to the fact squirrels tend to settle down in a general area, odds are if I go on another walk I will likely run into this same squirrel again some time.

description: Phylum: chordata

The squirrel's total body length measures 45 to 70 cm (17.7 to 27.6 in), tail length is 20 to 33 cm (7.9 to 13.0 in), and they range in weight from 500 to 1,000 grams (1.1 to 2.2 lb).[4] There is no sexual dimorphism in size or appearance. Individuals tend to be smaller in the west. There are three distinct geographical phases in coloration: In most areas the animals upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside, while in eastern regions such as the Appalachians there are more strikingly-patterned dark brown and black squirrels with white bands on the face and tail. In the south can be found isolated communities with uniform black coats. To help with climbing, they have sharp claws, developed extensors of digits and flexors of forearms, and abdominal musculature. Fox squirrels have excellent vision and well-developed senses of hearing and smell. They use scent marking to communicate with other fox squirrels. "Fox squirrels also have several sets of vibrissae, hairs or whiskers that are used as touch receptors to sense the environment. These are found above and below their eyes, on their chin and nose, and on each forearm."

The fox squirrel's natural range extends through most of the eastern United States, north into the southern prairie provinces of Canada, and west to the Dakotas, Colorado, and Texas. They are absent (except for vagrants) in New England, New Jersey, most of New York, northern and eastern Pennsylvania, Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces of Canada. They have been introduced to both northern and southern California,Oregon, Idaho, Montana,Washington, and New Mexico. While very versatile in their habitat choices, fox squirrels are most often found in forest patches of 40 hectares or less with an open understory, or in urban neighborhoods with trees. They thrive best among oak, hickory, walnut, pecan and pine trees, storing their nuts for winter. Western range extensions in Great Plains regions such as Kansas are associated with riverine corridors of cottonwood. A subspecies native to several eastern US states is the Delmarva fox squirrel (S. n. cinereus).

The UNT Pecan Creek Pollinative Prairie sits at the upper portion of the Pecan Creek watershed that flows to Northlakes Park, through Denton, collects the municipal wastewater treatment plant effluent, and then empties into Lewisville Lake.

description: The Fox squirrel was just chilling out on Tri-Hall Lawn. It was eating like a piece of cookie that it found on the ground and was just sitting in the middle of the lawn just eating it. It was all alone by itself just eating then scurried along up a nearby tree. The weather was just sunny, not very many clouds or any rain to worry about. It was an angled grass plain and surrounded by pine and oak trees. There were also some birds and all that flying about but nothing too spectacular. The Fox squirrel has red-orange coloration on the front of his/her belly all the way up to his/her face and ears as well as the underside of his/her tail. It has grey-ish coloration everywhere else. Which is how I identified the species of squirrel as well as just deduct by the region they can live at which is many places, but was also sharing with not too many squirrels. I noticed that they prefer being alone and aren’t really looking for any companionship or rely on any other fox squirrel. Reading about it, it does say they prefer to be alone and asocial, only really being around one another when they are mating. They are non-territorial, so by that extent they won’t fight each other over location, if anything they will fight over food. It also says that they actually prefer to be on the ground instead of being in trees. Which makes me wonder if they ever have any predators trying to prey on them, do they really think it’s a good idea to stay on the ground? Here at Cornell, they don’t usually have a problem with predators, but out in the middle of a forest, it is just a thought. They usually prefer nuts because they know the longevity of how they can preserve their food for later times.
